account: On 29 November 2023 Google DeepMind published GNoME in Nature. It reported 2.2 million structures below the convex hull, calling it “an order-of-magnitude expansion in stable materials known to humanity”. It stated that 736 of the stable structures had already been independently realized. The company blog adds that the A-Lab at Berkeley Lab synthesized more than 41 materials from the predictions. Leeman, Schoop, Palgrave and colleagues, of Princeton University and University College London, examined the 43 products of the A-Lab in PRX Energy on 7 March 2024. They concluded that no new materials had been made. Cheetham and Seshadri, of the University of California, Santa Barbara, examined the listings in Chemistry of Materials on 8 April 2024. They reported “scant evidence for compounds that fulfill the trifecta of novelty, credibility, and utility”. On 11 April 2024 404 Media quoted Cheetham as saying that the paper “falls way short” as a practical contribution. It quoted DeepMind as saying that it stands by all claims. In Scientific Reports on 29 July 2025, Widdowson and Kurlin, of the University of Liverpool, matched the 43 A-Lab crystals against the Inorganic Crystal Structure Database and the Materials Project. They found close existing neighbors for them and traced the near-duplicates to the step that substituted atoms in existing crystals. In ACS Materials Au on 20 October 2025, a team that includes Kristin Persson, who directs the Materials Project, reported that it had screened 44,651 GNoME structures. They highlighted two candidates, one never made and one made only in a disordered form. In Advanced Materials on 23 October 2025, Jakob, Walsh and colleagues estimated that 80% to 84% of GNoME entries may form disordered crystals. On 9 October 2026 Vitaliy Kurlin and colleagues at the University of Liverpool posted an analysis on arXiv, and Chemical & Engineering News reported it on 15 October 2026. The authors found more than 15% near-duplicates within GNoME, about 24% duplicating Materials Project entries and about 17% close to entries in the Inorganic Crystal Structure Database. Leslie Schoop of Princeton called some entries “completely unrealistic”. The Nature paper carries no correction.

ai_role.statement: The makers report that the graph networks filtered candidate structures and that DFT calculations then checked their stability. Over six rounds of active learning, the share of filtered structural candidates that DFT confirmed as stable rose from under 6% to over 80%. Candidates came from substitutions of atoms in known crystals and from random structure search. Widdowson and Kurlin trace near-duplicates of A-Lab products in older databases to the substitution step. No source isolates a contribution of the model to any material that was made and used.

display.answer: Google DeepMind's GNoME proposed 2.2 million crystal structures (380,000 stable); independent reviews (Cheetham & Seshadri 2024, Kurlin 2026) find duplicates and scant evidence of useful compounds. Counts of predicted stable structures do not establish distinct, useful, synthesizable materials. Concurrent experimental realizations are not necessarily caused by GNoME, and the retained critiques raise duplication and plausibility concerns that require direct reconciliation. The graph-network model is the vendor's. Its predictions are documented in a vendor-authored Nature paper and blog. Independent reviewers (Cheetham & Seshadri 2024; Kurlin 2026 as reported by C&EN) report near-duplicates, unrealistic compounds and little evidence of useful novel materials. Benefit therefore rests on the vendor's account and is contested.

fields.account: On 29 November 2023 Google DeepMind published GNoME in Nature. It reported 2.2 million structures below the convex hull, calling it “an order-of-magnitude expansion in stable materials known to humanity”. It stated that 736 of the stable structures had already been independently realized. The company blog adds that the A-Lab at Berkeley Lab synthesized more than 41 materials from the predictions. Leeman, Schoop, Palgrave and colleagues, of Princeton University and University College London, examined the 43 products of the A-Lab in PRX Energy on 7 March 2024. They concluded that no new materials had been made. Cheetham and Seshadri, of the University of California, Santa Barbara, examined the listings in Chemistry of Materials on 8 April 2024. They reported “scant evidence for compounds that fulfill the trifecta of novelty, credibility, and utility”. On 11 April 2024 404 Media quoted Cheetham as saying that the paper “falls way short” as a practical contribution. It quoted DeepMind as saying that it stands by all claims. In Scientific Reports on 29 July 2025, Widdowson and Kurlin, of the University of Liverpool, matched the 43 A-Lab crystals against the Inorganic Crystal Structure Database and the Materials Project. They found close existing neighbors for them and traced the near-duplicates to the step that substituted atoms in existing crystals. In ACS Materials Au on 20 October 2025, a team that includes Kristin Persson, who directs the Materials Project, reported that it had screened 44,651 GNoME structures. They highlighted two candidates, one never made and one made only in a disordered form. In Advanced Materials on 23 October 2025, Jakob, Walsh and colleagues estimated that 80% to 84% of GNoME entries may form disordered crystals. On 9 October 2026 Vitaliy Kurlin and colleagues at the University of Liverpool posted an analysis on arXiv, and Chemical & Engineering News reported it on 15 October 2026. The authors found more than 15% near-duplicates within GNoME, about 24% duplicating Materials Project entries and about 17% close to entries in the Inorganic Crystal Structure Database. Leslie Schoop of Princeton called some entries “completely unrealistic”. The Nature paper carries no correction.
